title: Brain
summary: The brain is the body's control center, a 1.3-1.4 kg organ of about 86 billion neurons.

layers.basics: Your brain handles everything you sense, think, feel and do. It is soft, wrinkled and floats in protective fluid inside the skull.
layers.deeper: It has a cerebrum (two hemispheres joined by the corpus callosum), cerebellum and brainstem. The outer folded layer, the cortex, handles complex functions; deeper structures regulate emotion, memory and body state.
layers.expert: Gray matter holds neuronal cell bodies and synapses; white matter is myelinated tracts. The cortex has six layers in most regions and is organized into functionally specialized but interconnected networks. Cerebrospinal fluid and the blood-brain barrier protect it. A proposed 'glymphatic' route along blood vessels may help clear waste, but it rests mainly on animal work and its mechanism is still debated.

facts: ≈ 8.6×10^10 (86.1 ± 8.1 billion; Azevedo et al. 2009, 4 adult male brains)
did_you_know: The brain's power draw is about that of a dim light bulb.
open_questions: How do patterns of neural activity give rise to subjective experience (the 'hard problem')?
How does the brain represent and store memories at the level of circuits and synapses?
Does the 'glymphatic' perivascular clearance route work in humans as it appears to in rodents, and what drives the fluid flow?

title: Frontal lobe
summary: The front part of the cortex for planning, decisions and voluntary movement.

layers.basics: The frontal lobe helps you plan, make choices, control impulses and start movements. Speech production relies on regions here (usually left).
layers.deeper: Contains the primary motor cortex, premotor areas and the prefrontal cortex. Broca's area supports speech production.
layers.expert: Prefrontal cortex continues to mature (thinning, myelination) into the twenties, and the end point varies by measure and person; dorsolateral PFC supports working memory and executive control, orbitofrontal PFC value computation. Motor homunculus is a somatotopic map along the precentral gyrus.

did_you_know: Frontal lobes are among the last brain regions to finish maturing.

title: Parietal lobe
summary: The upper-middle cortex that processes touch and body position and builds spatial awareness.

layers.basics: This lobe integrates touch, pressure and spatial information so you know where your body and objects are.
layers.deeper: The somatosensory cortex lies in the postcentral gyrus; posterior parietal areas guide reaching and attention.
layers.expert: Dorsal visual stream ('where/how') runs through the posterior parietal cortex; lesions can cause neglect or apraxia.

did_you_know: Damage to the right parietal lobe can make a person ignore the left half of the world.

title: Temporal lobe
summary: The side cortex for hearing, language comprehension and memory.

layers.basics: Sounds, spoken words and faces are processed on the sides of the brain, near the ears.
layers.deeper: Contains the auditory cortex, Wernicke's area and the hippocampus deep inside.
layers.expert: Ventral visual stream (object, face recognition) in inferotemporal cortex; medial temporal structures are essential for declarative memory.

did_you_know: Temporal lobe damage can leave people unable to recognize faces.

title: Occipital lobe
summary: The rear cortex dedicated mostly to vision.

layers.basics: The back of your brain is wired to turn signals from your eyes into what you see.
layers.deeper: Primary visual cortex (V1) receives input from the thalamus and maps the visual field.
layers.expert: V1 is retinotopic with cortical magnification of the fovea; later areas contribute to orientation, form, colour (notably V4) and motion (notably V5/MT), with substantial overlap between them.

did_you_know: Electrically stimulating the visual cortex of awake patients produces small spots of light called phosphenes. A blow to the head can also make people 'see stars', but how it does so is not settled.

title: Cerebral cortex
summary: The wrinkled outer sheet of the brain where much of perception, thought and voluntary action is computed.

layers.basics: The thin, folded outer layer of your brain. The folds let a large sheet fit inside the skull.
layers.deeper: About 16 billion neurons sit in a sheet 2-4 mm thick; folds (gyri and sulci) give it an area of roughly 2,000 cm².
layers.expert: Six-layer neocortical architecture with canonical microcircuits; layer 5 pyramidal neurons project subcortically; cortical areas defined by cytoarchitecture (Brodmann) and multimodal parcellations.

did_you_know: If you unfolded the cortex it would cover roughly 0.2 m², about the area of a large dinner napkin.

title: Hippocampus
summary: A seahorse-shaped structure needed to form new long-term memories.

layers.basics: The hippocampus helps turn experiences into lasting memories and helps you find your way.
layers.deeper: Part of the limbic system, it contains place cells and is central to forming episodic memories.
layers.expert: Trisynaptic circuit (EC-DG-CA3-CA1); LTP at Schaffer collaterals; one of few sites of adult neurogenesis (extent in adult humans is debated).

did_you_know: London taxi drivers' studies found enlarged posterior hippocampi, linked to navigation experience.
open_questions: Does substantial adult hippocampal neurogenesis occur in humans?

title: Hypothalamus
summary: A small brain region that regulates temperature, hunger, thirst, sleep and hormones.

layers.basics: This almond-sized region keeps your body's internal settings steady and controls the pituitary gland.
layers.deeper: It links the nervous system to the endocrine system via the pituitary stalk.
layers.expert: Contains nuclei such as the suprachiasmatic (circadian clock), paraventricular and supraoptic (oxytocin/vasopressin) and arcuate (feeding, leptin).

did_you_know: It weighs about as much as a grape yet coordinates much of homeostasis.

title: Corpus callosum
summary: The thick band of nerve fibers that connects the brain's two hemispheres.

layers.basics: This bridge lets your left and right brain share information.
layers.deeper: About 200 million axons cross here.
layers.expert: Callosotomy for epilepsy produces 'split-brain' effects in specific tasks. Callosal fibers are mainly homotopic.

did_you_know: About 1 in 4,000 people are born without it (agenesis) and can seem normal in daily life, though testing often finds subtler difficulties with social and higher-order thinking.

title: Thalamus
summary: A relay hub that routes sensory signals to the cortex.

layers.basics: Nearly all senses except smell pass through the thalamus on the way to the cortex.
layers.deeper: It also takes part in sleep, attention and consciousness.
layers.expert: Thalamic nuclei (LGN, MGN, VPL/VPM) relay and gate sensory information; thalamocortical loops with reticular nucleus generate sleep spindles.

facts: a collection of nuclei that relay signals between cortex and the rest of the nervous system
did_you_know: Smell is the one major sense whose signals reach the cortex without first passing through the thalamus.

title: Amygdala
summary: An almond-shaped cluster of nuclei that helps detect threats and tag memories with emotion.

layers.basics: This small region reacts fast to frightening or emotionally important things.
layers.deeper: It links with the hypothalamus and brainstem to produce fear responses.
layers.expert: Basolateral and central nuclei mediate fear conditioning; roles in emotion are broader than 'fear center'.

facts: medial temporal lobe, next to the hippocampus
did_you_know: The name is Greek for almond.
open_questions: How much of the amygdala's role is specific to fear, and how much is general emotional or salience processing?
How well do findings from rodent fear-conditioning circuits carry over to the human amygdala?

title: Basal ganglia
summary: Deep brain nuclei that help select and start movements and habits.

layers.basics: These deep structures help you start and smooth out movement and learn routines.
layers.deeper: Loss of dopamine neurons in this system leads to Parkinson's disease.
layers.expert: Cortico-basal ganglia-thalamic loops with direct/indirect pathways; dopamine from the substantia nigra modulates them.

facts: caudate, putamen, globus pallidus (closely linked to the subthalamic nucleus and the substantia nigra)
did_you_know: In a post-mortem study of Parkinson's disease, pigmented dopamine neurons of the substantia nigra were lost fastest early on, about 45% in the first decade of illness.

title: Cerebellum
summary: The 'little brain' at the back that coordinates movement and balance.

layers.basics: The cerebellum fine-tunes your movements so they are smooth and accurate.
layers.deeper: It contains about 80% of the brain's neurons, most of them tiny granule cells.
layers.expert: Compares intended and actual movement via forward models; Purkinje cells are inhibitory output of the cortex; roles in cognition and timing.

did_you_know: It holds around 80% of all neurons in the brain though it is a tenth of the mass.

title: Brainstem
summary: The stalk connecting brain to spinal cord that controls breathing, heartbeat and wakefulness.

layers.basics: The brainstem runs the basic life functions you never think about.
layers.deeper: It includes midbrain, pons and medulla and most cranial nerves.
layers.expert: Reticular formation regulates arousal; medullary respiratory groups (preBötzinger complex) generate rhythm; cardiovascular centers regulate pressure.

did_you_know: Brainstem death is the legal criterion of death in some countries.

title: Spinal cord
summary: A cable of nerve tissue running down the spine, carrying signals between brain and body.

layers.basics: The spinal cord is the main data highway between the brain and the body and runs simple reflexes itself.
layers.deeper: Dorsal roots carry sensory input, ventral roots carry motor output, with 31 pairs of spinal nerves.
layers.expert: Butterfly-shaped gray matter with dorsal, intermediate, ventral horns; ascending (dorsal column, spinothalamic) and descending (corticospinal) tracts.

did_you_know: The spinal cord is only as thick as a finger.

title: Peripheral nerves
summary: Cables of axons that connect the CNS to every part of the body.

layers.basics: Nerves are bundles of long nerve fibers that carry commands out and sensations in.
layers.deeper: 12 cranial and 31 spinal nerve pairs, and many fibers are wrapped in myelin by Schwann cells for speed, while others (such as C fibers) are unmyelinated and slow.
layers.expert: Fibers classified A-alpha to C by diameter and myelination; conduction velocities from 0.5 to 120 m/s; axons can regrow in the PNS (about 1 mm per day, often incompletely), whereas adult CNS axons regenerate very poorly.

did_you_know: The longest single nerve cells can have axons about a meter long.

title: Left eye
summary: The left eye focuses light onto the retina, where it becomes nerve signals.

layers.basics: The eye is a living camera: light enters through the clear front, is focused, and strikes light-sensing cells at the back.
layers.deeper: The cornea does most of the focusing and the lens fine-tunes it. The retina contains rods and cones. A left eye has the same structures as a right eye (cornea, iris, lens, vitreous humor, retina, fovea, optic nerve); descend through the right eye to explore them.
layers.expert: In a simple thin-lens model with a 2.0 cm lens-to-retina distance the eye's optical power is ≈ 50 D (D = dioptre, 1/m), about two-thirds of it from the cornea; photoreceptors transduce light via the rhodopsin-transducin-PDE cascade, and retinal ganglion cells project to the LGN and superior colliculus.

did_you_know: The eye's retina is technically part of the brain, grown out from the embryonic forebrain.

title: Right eye
summary: The right eye focuses light onto the retina, where it becomes nerve signals.

layers.basics: The eye is a living camera: light enters through the clear front, is focused, and strikes light-sensing cells at the back.
layers.deeper: The cornea does most of the focusing and the lens fine-tunes it. The retina contains rods and cones.
layers.expert: In a simple thin-lens model with a 2.0 cm lens-to-retina distance the eye's optical power is ≈ 50 D (D = dioptre, 1/m), about two-thirds of it from the cornea; photoreceptors transduce light via the rhodopsin-transducin-PDE cascade, and retinal ganglion cells project to the LGN and superior colliculus.

did_you_know: The eye's retina is technically part of the brain, grown out from the embryonic forebrain.

title: Cornea
summary: The clear dome at the front of the eye that does most of its focusing.

layers.basics: The transparent window of the eye. It bends light the most, about two-thirds of the eye's focusing power.
layers.deeper: It has no blood vessels, so it gets oxygen straight from the air and tears, and it is very sensitive to touch.
layers.expert: Five layers (epithelium, Bowman's layer, stroma, Descemet's membrane, endothelium); stromal transparency relies on regular collagen fibril spacing (<λ/2).

facts: Share of the eye's focusing power
did_you_know: Corneal grafts are rarely rejected in low-risk eyes, helped by the cornea having no blood vessels and sitting in an immune-privileged eye. Rejection is still a problem in high-risk eyes where vessels have grown into the cornea.

title: Iris
summary: The colored ring that controls pupil size.

layers.basics: The iris opens and closes the pupil to adjust how much light enters.
layers.deeper: Smooth muscles contract the pupil in bright light (sphincter) or enlarge it in dark (dilator).
layers.expert: Eye color arises from melanin in the anterior stroma; parasympathetic via CN III, sympathetic via the superior cervical ganglion.

facts: sphincter (narrows the pupil) and dilator (widens it)
did_you_know: Iris texture is so distinctive that it is used for biometric identification; a person's left and right irises differ from each other as much as unrelated irises do.

title: Lens
summary: A clear flexible disc that fine-tunes focus.

layers.basics: The lens changes shape so you can switch between near and far objects.
layers.deeper: For near focus the ciliary muscle contracts and the lens becomes thicker and more powerful; for distance the muscle relaxes and the lens is thinner (accommodation).
layers.expert: Lens fibers lose their organelles and are packed with crystallin proteins; presbyopia, the loss of near focus with age, arises as the lens stiffens.

facts: Share of the eye's focusing power
≈ 1/3, and the only part that adjusts
did_you_know: Lens crystallin proteins last a lifetime without replacement.

title: Vitreous humor
summary: A clear gel filling the main chamber of the eye.

layers.basics: A jelly that keeps the eyeball round.
layers.deeper: Mostly water, held in a sparse network of collagen fibrils and hyaluronan.
layers.expert: Age-related syneresis leads to 'floaters' and posterior vitreous detachment.

facts: the posterior cavity, behind the lens
did_you_know: Floaters are shadows of vitreous fibers on your retina.

title: Retina
summary: The light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye.

layers.basics: The retina turns images into nerve signals using about a hundred million light-sensing cells.
layers.deeper: Contains rods, cones, and neurons that begin image processing before the signal leaves the eye.
layers.expert: Layers: photoreceptors, bipolar, horizontal, amacrine and ganglion cells; image is inverted.

did_you_know: The retina processes information before sending it to the brain.

title: Fovea
summary: The tiny pit in the retina with the sharpest vision.

layers.basics: Where you look directly, light lands on the fovea, packed with cones.
layers.deeper: It supplies the high-resolution color vision you use for reading.
layers.expert: Peak cone density averages ≈ 2×10^5 cones/mm² (about 1.0-3.2×10^5 between people) and the central ≈ 0.35 mm has no rods (Curcio et al. 1990). Cones there connect mainly through the midget pathway, roughly one cone to one midget bipolar cell to one midget ganglion cell.

did_you_know: Only about 1-2 degrees of your visual field is truly sharp.

title: Optic nerve
summary: The bundle of about a million fibers carrying visual signals to the brain.

layers.basics: The cable from the eye to the brain.
layers.deeper: It leaves at the optic disc, which has no photoreceptors, creating the blind spot.
layers.expert: Myelinated by oligodendrocytes (CNS tract); about 10^6 axons (the count varies between people and falls by roughly 4,000 per year with age); partial decussation at the optic chiasm.

did_you_know: Each of your eyes has a blind spot your brain fills in.
